questions.question: Who was the first President of the Indian National Congress?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee** was the first President of the Indian National Congress (INC), presiding over its inaugural session in 1885.
 
• The first session of the INC was held in **Bombay (now Mumbai)** from 28–31 December 1885.
 
• This historic session was attended by **72 delegates**, marking the beginning of the Indian National Congress as a political platform.
 
• Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee was a prominent lawyer and statesman, deeply involved in the Indian freedom struggle.
 
• The INC was founded by **A.O. Hume**, a retired British civil servant, with the aim of providing a platform for civil and political dialogue among Indians.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Congress (INC):**

 
 
• Founded on 28 December 1885, the INC was one of the most significant political organizations in India's struggle for independence.
 
• The founders included A.O. Hume, Dadabhai Naoroji, and Dinshaw Wacha.
 
• The INC initially aimed at creating a dialogue with the British government for reforms but later evolved into a mass movement for complete independence.
 
 
 
• **Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee:**
 
 
• He was the first Indian to act as an Advocate-General of Bengal and the first Indian to contest elections for the British Parliament.
 
• Bonnerjee played a pivotal role in the early years of the INC, helping shape its policies and direction.
 
 
 
• **Key Goals of Early INC:**
 
 
• The early INC worked towards greater representation of Indians in administrative roles, reduction of military expenditure, and promotion of Indian industries.
 
• It sought constitutional reforms and civil rights for Indians under British rule.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of INC:**
 
 
• The INC played a central role in India's independence movement, with leaders like Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, and Sardar Patel emerging from its ranks.
 
• It continues to be a major political party in India post-independence.

questions.question: Who among the following chose the path of forming the army 'Azad Hind Fauj' to liberate India from the clutches of the British?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Subhas Chandra Bose**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Subhas Chandra Bose was a prominent Indian nationalist whose defiant patriotism made him a hero in India.
 
• He formed the Indian National Army (INA), also known as Azad Hind Fauj, in 1942 with the help of Japan during World War II.
 
• The INA aimed to secure Indian independence from British rule through armed struggle.
 
• Bose's famous slogan was "Give me blood, and I shall give you freedom!" which inspired many Indians to join the freedom movement.
 
• He was a key figure in the Indian independence movement and is remembered for his militant approach and leadership of the INA.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Formation of INA**

 
 
• The Indian National Army was initially formed in 1942 under the leadership of Captain Mohan Singh.
 
• It was later reorganized by Subhas Chandra Bose in 1943 after his arrival in Southeast Asia.
 
• The INA drew its soldiers from Indian prisoners of war captured by Japanese forces in Singapore and other Southeast Asian regions.
 
 
 
• **Azad Hind Government**
 
 
• Subhas Chandra Bose proclaimed the formation of the Provisional Government of Free India, or Azad Hind, on October 21, 1943.
 
• This government was recognized by Axis powers including Japan, Germany, and Italy.
 
• Bose served as the Head of State, Prime Minister, and Minister of War of this provisional government.
 
 
 
• **Bose's Leadership and Legacy**
 
 
• Bose's leadership in the INA was pivotal in rallying Indian expatriates and POWs to fight against British colonial rule.
 
• He remains a highly respected and influential figure in Indian history for his dedication and sacrifice for India's independence.
 
 
 
• **INA's Military Campaigns**
 
 
• The INA fought alongside Japanese forces in the Burma Campaign against the British Indian Army.
 
• They participated in key battles such as the Battle of Imphal and the Battle of Kohima in 1944.
 
• Despite initial successes, the INA eventually faced defeat due to logistical challenges and the larger Allied counter-offensive.

questions.question: Who among the following was sent to India in March 1942 to seek the cooperation of the Indian political groups?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Stafford Cripps**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Stafford Cripps was sent to India in March 1942 by the British government to seek the cooperation of Indian political groups.
 
• The mission was known as the Cripps Mission.
 
• His main objective was to negotiate with Indian leaders and secure their support for the British war efforts in World War II.
 
• The mission proposed granting India dominion status after the war, with the right to secede from the British Commonwealth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cripps Mission:**

 
 
• It was a failed attempt by the British government to secure Indian cooperation during World War II.
 
• The proposal included provisions for Indian self-governance but was rejected by Indian leaders.
 
• Indian National Congress and the Muslim League had conflicting interests, contributing to the mission's failure.
 
• The mission's failure led to increased demand for complete independence, eventually resulting in the Quit India Movement.
 
 
 
• **Stafford Cripps:**
 
 
• He was a British Labour politician known for his diplomatic efforts during World War II.
 
• Cripps held various high-ranking positions, including Chancellor of the Exchequer.
 
• He was known for his left-wing views and support for Indian self-governance.
 
• Despite the failure of his mission, he remained an influential figure in British politics.
 
 
 
• **Dominion Status:**
 
 
• Dominion status meant a nation within the British Commonwealth with autonomous control over its domestic and foreign affairs.
 
• It was seen as a stepping stone towards full independence.
 
• Countries like Canada, Australia, and New Zealand were granted dominion status before becoming fully independent.
 
• Cripps proposed dominion status for India post-World War II, which was rejected by Indian leaders seeking complete independence.

questions.question: Which of the following Acts was based on the Mountbatten plan?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Indian Independence Act, 1947**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Indian Independence Act, 1947** was based on the proposals of the **Mountbatten Plan**, which outlined the partition of British India into two independent dominions – India and Pakistan.
 
• The Act received royal assent on **18th July 1947** and came into effect on **15th August 1947**, marking India's independence from British rule.
 
• It provided for the **division of British India** into two separate nations and granted both dominions the right to secede from the British Commonwealth.
 
• The Act abolished the sovereignty of the British Crown over Indian princely states, allowing them to choose to join India or Pakistan or remain independent.
 
• The **Constituent Assemblies** of both India and Pakistan were empowered to frame their respective constitutions and legislate as sovereign bodies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mountbatten Plan**

 
 
• Proposed by the last Viceroy of India, **Lord Louis Mountbatten**, in June 1947.
 
• It recommended the partition of British India into India and Pakistan based on religious majorities.
 
• The princely states were given the option to join either dominion or remain independent.
 
 
 
• **Partition of India**
 
 
• Led to the creation of two nations: India (predominantly Hindu) and Pakistan (predominantly Muslim).
 
• Resulted in one of the largest human migrations in history, with an estimated 10-15 million people displaced.
 
• Accompanied by widespread communal violence, leading to significant loss of life and property.
 
 
 
• **Indian Independence Act Provisions**
 
 
• Ended British rule in India and declared India and Pakistan as independent sovereign states.
 
• Provided for the division of assets, including military forces, between the two nations.
 
• Terminated the jurisdiction of the British Parliament over Indian affairs.
 
 
 
• **Role of Lord Mountbatten**
 
 
• Served as the last Viceroy of India and the first Governor-General of independent India.
 
• Played a key role in managing the transition of power and the partition process.

questions.question: Who wrote the book 'The Indian War of Independence' related to Indian nationalist history of the 1857 revolt?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**V D Savarkar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Vinayak Damodar Savarkar**, commonly known as V D Savarkar, was a prominent Indian freedom fighter and nationalist.
 
• He authored the book **'The Indian War of Independence'** in 1909, which is an account of the 1857 revolt.
 
• This book is considered a significant work in Indian nationalist history and provides a detailed analysis of the first major rebellion against British rule.
 
• V D Savarkar was also a proponent of Hindutva and played a crucial role in the freedom struggle through his writings and revolutionary activities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **1857 Revolt**

 
 
• The 1857 revolt, also known as the First War of Indian Independence, was a major uprising against the British East India Company.
 
• It began on 10 May 1857 in Meerut and spread to various parts of India including Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, and Jhansi.
 
• The revolt was characterized by widespread military and civilian discontent against British policies, including land reforms and social changes.
 
• Key figures included Rani Lakshmibai, Bahadur Shah Zafar, Nana Sahib, and Tatya Tope.
 
 
 
• **Hindutva**
 
 
• Hindutva is an ideology seeking to establish the hegemony of Hindus in the Indian subcontinent.
 
• V D Savarkar is credited with conceptualizing and promoting Hindutva through his writings and political activities.
 
• The term was first used in Savarkar's pamphlet titled 'Hindutva: Who is a Hindu?' published in 1923.
 
• It emphasizes cultural unity and the revival of Hindu traditions and values.
 
 
 
• **Vinayak Damodar Savarkar**
 
 
• Born on 28 May 1883 in Bhagur, Nashik, Maharashtra, Savarkar was a poet, writer, and politician.
 
• He was arrested in 1909 for his revolutionary activities and was sentenced to life imprisonment in the Andaman cellular jail.
 
• After his release in 1924, he continued to be active in politics and social reforms.
 
• He passed away on 26 February 1966.

• Founded in 1929 by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the movement was based on the principles of non-violence and was dedicated to social and political reform.
 
• Members of the movement, known as "Red Shirts," were committed to peaceful resistance against British rule.
 
 
 
• **Non-Violent Resistance**
 
 
• Inspired by Mahatma Gandhi, Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan promoted non-violent resistance as a powerful tool for achieving social and political change.
 
• He believed that true strength lay in the ability to endure suffering without resorting to violence.
 
 
 
• **Legacy and Influence**
 
 
• Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's legacy as "Frontier Gandhi" continues to inspire peace activists around the world.

questions.question: What was the birthplace of Rani Laxmibai, one of the freedom fighters of the First War of Independence of 1857?

__
 
• Rani Laxmibai, also known as the Queen of Jhansi, was born on **19 November 1828** in **Varanasi**, Uttar Pradesh, India.
 
• Her birth name was **Manikarnika Tambe**, and she was affectionately called "Manu" in her childhood.
 
• She was married to Maharaja Gangadhar Rao of Jhansi in 1842, after which she became known as Rani Laxmibai.
 
• Rani Laxmibai is remembered as one of the most iconic leaders of the **First War of Independence in 1857**, where she played a pivotal role in the resistance against British colonial rule.
 
• Her valor and leadership during the Siege of Jhansi made her a symbol of resistance and patriotism in Indian history.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **First War of Independence (1857):**

 
 
• Also referred to as the Sepoy Mutiny or the Indian Rebellion of 1857, it marked the first large-scale resistance against British rule in India.
 
• The revolt was triggered by various factors, including political annexation, economic exploitation, and cultural imposition by the British East India Company.
 
• Rani Laxmibai was one of the prominent leaders, along with others like Tatya Tope, Nana Sahib, and Bahadur Shah II.
 
 
 
• **Doctrine of Lapse:**
 
 
• A controversial policy introduced by Lord Dalhousie, the Governor-General of India (1848–1856).
 
• Under this doctrine, the British annexed Indian princely states if the ruler died without a male heir.
 
• This policy led to the annexation of Jhansi, which became a primary reason for Rani Laxmibai's rebellion against British rule.
 
 
 
• **Legacy of Rani Laxmibai:**
 
 
• Her courage and sacrifice have been immortalized in Indian history, and she remains a symbol of resistance and empowerment.
 
• Her famous quote, "Main Apni Jhansi Nahi Doongi" ("I will not give up my Jhansi"), is remembered as a testament to her determination.
 
 
 
• **Statues and Memorials:**
 
 
• Numerous statues of Rani Laxmibai have been erected across India as a tribute to her bravery.
 
• The Rani Jhansi Marine National Park, located in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, is named in her honor.

questions.question: In 1930, who in his most famous speech stressed the creation of a Muslim state in North West India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sir Muhammad Iqbal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Sir Muhammad Iqbal, a renowned philosopher, poet, and politician in British India, is known for his influential role in the creation of Pakistan.
 
• In his famous Allahabad Address in 1930, Iqbal proposed the idea of a separate Muslim state in the northwest of India, which laid the foundation for Pakistan.
 
• Iqbal's vision was for a federated state with autonomous Muslim-majority regions, ensuring the protection of Muslim identity and interests.
 
• This address became a significant milestone in the history of the Indian subcontinent, leading to the eventual establishment of Pakistan in 1947.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Allahabad Address (1930)**

 
 
• The speech was delivered at the annual session of the All India Muslim League.
 
• Iqbal articulated the need for a separate Muslim state, emphasizing cultural and religious differences between Muslims and Hindus.
 
• This address is often regarded as the conceptual foundation for the creation of Pakistan.
 
 
 
• **Two-Nation Theory**
 
 
• The idea that Muslims and Hindus are two distinct nations, with their own customs, religion, and traditions, and therefore, should have separate homelands.
 
• Iqbal's vision in the Allahabad Address was a precursor to the Two-Nation Theory.
 
 
 
• **Sir Muhammad Iqbal's Contributions**
 
 
• Iqbal is also celebrated for his literary works, including Persian and Urdu poetry that inspire Muslim identity and pride.

questions.question: How did the drain of wealth theory, as proposed by Dadabhai Naoroji, explain India’s poverty under British rule?

options.text: Export of Indian resources and wealth to Britain without fair compensation

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Export of Indian resources and wealth to Britain without fair compensation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji's "Drain of Wealth" theory argued that British colonial policies led to the systematic exploitation of India's resources, transferring wealth to Britain without adequate compensation.
 
• The British extracted economic surplus through unfair trade practices, including exporting raw materials like cotton and indigo, while flooding Indian markets with British manufactured goods.
 
• Taxes collected in India were used to pay for administrative expenses, salaries, and pensions of British officials, instead of being reinvested in India's development.
 
• The theory highlighted that capital and profits generated in India were expatriated to Britain, leading to a lack of funds for industrial and agricultural growth in India.
 
• This exploitation created widespread poverty and stagnation in India while enriching Britain, as documented in Naoroji's book "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India" (1901).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Drain of Wealth Theory:** Proposed by Dadabhai Naoroji in the late 19th century, it emphasized the economic exploitation of India under British rule.
 
• **Economic Surplus:** The portion of India's production that was not reinvested in the country but transferred to Britain, leading to economic stagnation.
 
• **Home Charges:** Expenses such as salaries, military costs, pensions, and debt servicing paid by India to Britain, which were part of the economic "drain."
 
• **Impact:** The theory revealed how colonial policies depleted India's wealth, contributing to widespread poverty and lack of development during British rule.
 
• **Legacy:** The Drain of Wealth theory became one of the foundational arguments for India's independence movement, inspiring leaders to demand economic justice and sovereignty.

questions.question: Which of the following Acts provided for the establishment of an All-India Federation consisting of provinces and princely states as units?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Government of India Act, 1935**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Government of India Act, 1935 provided for the establishment of an All-India Federation consisting of provinces and princely states as units.
 
• This Act marked a significant shift from the previous Acts by proposing a federation and granting more autonomy to Indian provinces.
 
• It introduced provincial autonomy and proposed a federal structure, though the federation never came into being due to the lack of agreement from the princely states.
 
• The Act also introduced direct elections, thereby increasing the number of Indians who could vote.
 
• It was the last pre-independence constitution of India and remained in effect until the Constitution of India came into force in 1950.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Provincial Autonomy:**

 
 
• The Act allowed provinces to act as autonomous units of administration in their defined spheres.
 
• Provincial governments were given more control over various departments and subjects.
 
• Governors were now required to act on the advice of ministers responsible to the provincial legislatures.
 
 
 
• **Federal Structure:**
 
 
• The Act proposed a federal structure with a central government and provincial governments.
 
• The federation was to include both British Indian provinces and princely states.
 
• However, the federation never materialized as the princely states did not join.
 
 
 
• **Reserved and Transferred Subjects:**
 
 
• The Act divided subjects into 'Reserved' and 'Transferred' categories.
 
• Reserved subjects were administered by the Governor on behalf of the Crown, while transferred subjects were administered by ministers responsible to the legislatures.
 
 
 
• **Introduction of Direct Elections:**
 
 
• The Act expanded the electorate and introduced direct elections for the first time.
 
• This increased the number of Indians eligible to vote, laying the groundwork for future democratic processes.

• It introduced the concept of **provincial autonomy**, granting provinces the power to govern themselves in areas such as agriculture, health, and education.

questions.question: Which extremist leader became a symbol of martyrdom after his death in British custody?

• The declaration marked the Indian National Congress's resolve to fight for full independence from British rule.

• It was often referred to as the "**party within the Congress**" because it operated under the umbrella of the **Indian National Congress** but pursued a different strategy to achieve **Swaraj** (self-rule).
 
• The party sought to expose the inadequacies of British rule by participating in the legislative processes and advocating for **constitutional reforms.**
 
• Although the Swaraj Party eventually merged back into the Congress, its formation marked a significant phase in the **Indian freedom struggle** by showcasing diverse strategies for achieving independence.

questions.question: When did Mahatma Gandhi leave for England to participate in the Second Round Table Conference?

__
 
• Mahatma Gandhi left for England in **1931** to participate in the **Second Round Table Conference**.
 
• The Second Round Table Conference took place from **7 September to 1 December 1931**.
 
• It was conducted in **London** and aimed to discuss constitutional reforms in India.
 
• Gandhi attended as the **sole representative of the Indian National Congress**, advocating for complete independence (Purna Swaraj).
 
• Despite his efforts, the conference failed due to disagreements between various Indian leaders and the British government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Round Table Conferences:**

 
 
• Three Round Table Conferences were held between **1930 and 1932** to discuss India's constitutional future.
 
• The first was held in **1930**, but the Congress boycotted it.
 
• The second conference (1931) saw Gandhi's participation, but no consensus was reached.
 
• The third conference (1932) had limited Indian participation as Congress again boycotted it.
 
 
 
• **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931):**
 
 
• This agreement between Mahatma Gandhi and Lord Irwin led to Gandhi attending the Second Round Table Conference.
 
• The pact included the release of political prisoners and allowed Indians to make salt for personal use.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Conferences:**
 
 
• The conferences marked the first time Indian leaders were invited to discuss constitutional reforms on an international platform.
 
• Although they failed to produce immediate results, they highlighted the growing demand for Indian self-rule.
 
 
 
• **Outcome of the Second Round Table Conference:**
 
 
• No agreement was reached on dominion status or representation for minorities.
 
• The British government later introduced the **Communal Award** in 1932, exacerbating divisions within India.

questions.question: Lord Canning announced a Durbar after the Revolt of 1857 at:
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Lord Canning, the first Viceroy of India, announced a Durbar at **Allahabad** in 1858 following the Revolt of 1857.
 
• The event marked the formal proclamation of the transfer of power from the East India Company to the British Crown.
 
• At the Durbar, Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 was publicly read, which assured Indians of religious tolerance, equal treatment under the law, and non-interference in religious practices.
 
• The Proclamation also promised administrative reforms and emphasized the British Crown's commitment to justice and governance in India.
 
• The Durbar in Allahabad symbolized the end of the rule of the East India Company and the beginning of direct British governance in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The Revolt of 1857:**

 
 
• The Revolt of 1857, also known as the First War of Indian Independence, was a large-scale rebellion against the East India Company's rule.
 
• It was triggered by grievances related to political annexations, economic exploitation, and cultural interference.
 
• The rebellion was led by figures such as Rani Lakshmibai, Tatya Tope, Nana Sahib, and Bahadur Shah Zafar.
 
• While the revolt was eventually suppressed, it marked a turning point in Indian history.
 
 
 
• **Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858:**
 
 
• It was issued on 1 November 1858 and is often referred to as the "Magna Carta of India."
 
• The Proclamation declared that the British Crown would take over the governance of India from the East India Company.
 
• It assured Indians of non-interference in religious practices and equal treatment under British law.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Durbar at Allahabad:**
 
 
• The Durbar marked a significant shift in British policy in India, focusing on consolidation and governance rather than expansion.
 
• It sought to pacify Indian sentiments post-1857 and establish the British Crown's authority and legitimacy.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the 1857 Revolt on Administration:**
 
 
• The British Crown introduced administrative reforms to stabilize governance in India.
 
• The Indian Civil Service (ICS) was strengthened, and recruitment was opened to Indians, albeit with restrictive conditions.
 
• The British military was reorganized, with a greater emphasis on loyalty and European dominance in key positions.

questions.question: What is the main aspect of Gandhiji's ideology?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Truth-force**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Truth-force, also known as **Satyagraha**, was the cornerstone of Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy.
 
• Satyagraha emphasizes the power of truth and non-violence as tools for achieving social and political change.
 
• Gandhiji believed that truth (Satya) and non-violence (Ahimsa) were interconnected and essential for resolving conflicts.
 
• The ideology of Truth-force was applied by Gandhi during movements like the **Salt March (1930)** and the **Quit India Movement (1942)**.
 
• This principle inspires global movements advocating civil disobedience and peaceful resistance against injustice.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Satyagraha:** Derived from Sanskrit, meaning "holding onto truth," it rejects violence and focuses on moral strength.
 
• **Ahimsa:** Non-violence is a key element of Gandhian ideology and is rooted in ancient Indian traditions like Jainism and Buddhism.
 
• **Salt March:** A major act of civil disobedience led by Gandhi in 1930 to protest against British salt taxes.
 
• **Influence on Global Leaders:** Gandhi's Truth-force inspired figures like Martin Luther King Jr. and Nelson Mandela in their fight for civil rights and freedom.
 
• **Constructive Programs:** Along with Satyagraha, Gandhi advocated self-reliance, rural development, and education as means for societal reform.

questions.question: Which group criticised the moderates for their 'mendicancy'?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Extremists**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Extremists** were a group within the Indian National Congress (INC) who believed in more assertive and radical methods to achieve **Swaraj (self-rule)**.
 
• They criticised the **Moderates** for their policy of relying on petitions, prayers, and appeals to the **British government**, which they termed as acts of **'mendicancy' (begging)**.
 
• Prominent leaders of the Extremist faction included **Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and Bipin Chandra Pal**, collectively known as the **Lal-Bal-Pal** trio.
 
• The Extremists believed in methods such as **boycotting British goods, promoting Swadeshi (indigenous) industries, and mass mobilisation** to achieve their goals.
 
• Their criticism of the Moderates came from the belief that the latter's approach was **ineffective and overly submissive** to colonial rulers.
 
• The split between the Extremists and Moderates in the INC occurred during the **Surat Session of 1907**, reflecting their ideological differences.
 
• The Extremists played a significant role in inspiring **nationalist sentiments** among Indians and laying the groundwork for more radical movements in India's struggle for independence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **British Government**__

 __
 
• The **British government** was the colonial authority in India during this period.
 
• While the British government did not directly criticise the Moderates, they largely ignored or dismissed their demands for reforms and greater Indian representation.
 
• The British preferred the Moderates over the Extremists, as the latter's methods posed a more direct challenge to their rule.
 
 
 
• **Socialists**__
 __
 
• The **Socialist movement** in India gained momentum in the 1920s and 1930s, focusing on issues such as **economic equality and workers' rights**.
 
• Socialists were not a prominent political force during the time of the Moderates and Extremists' debates within the INC.
 
• They later influenced the Indian freedom struggle through leaders like **Jayaprakash Narayan and M.N. Roy**.
 
 
 
• **Constitutionalists**__
 
 
• **Constitutionalists** were those who sought reforms within the framework of the British legal and constitutional system.
 
• They were similar to the Moderates in their approach but were not a distinct group actively criticising either the Moderates or Extremists.
 
• They believed in achieving autonomy through **legal and constitutional means**, often working within colonial institutions.

questions.question: Who among the following was NOT associated with the 'moderate' phase of Indian National Congress?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bipin Chandra Pal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Bipin Chandra Pal** was associated with the **extremist phase** of the Indian National Congress, not the moderate phase.
 
• The extremist leaders, including Bipin Chandra Pal, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and Lala Lajpat Rai, advocated for **immediate self-rule** and were known as the "Lal-Bal-Pal" trio.
 
• In contrast, the moderates, such as Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, and Surendranath Banerjee, believed in achieving reforms through **constitutional means**.
 
• The moderate phase (1885–1905) of the Indian National Congress focused on **petitioning the British government** for gradual reforms, unlike the confrontational approach of extremists.
 
• Bipin Chandra Pal's role in the nationalist movement became prominent during the **Swadeshi Movement (1905–1911)**, which marked the beginning of the extremist phase.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Moderate Leaders of the INC:**

 
 
• Key moderate leaders include Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, and Surendranath Banerjee.
 
• The moderates believed in **dialogue, petitions, and resolutions** to influence British policy.
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji highlighted the concept of the **“Drain of Wealth”** in his book "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India."
 
 
 
• **Extremist Phase of the INC:**
 
 
• This phase (1905–1920) was marked by leaders like Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Lala Lajpat Rai.
 
• The extremists promoted the idea of **Swaraj (self-rule)** and actively opposed British policies.
 
 
 
• **Swadeshi Movement:**
 
 
• Launched in 1905 as a response to the **partition of Bengal** by the British.
 
• Encouraged the use of indigenous goods and boycotting British goods.
 
 
 
• **Indian National Congress (INC):**
 
 
• Founded in 1885, the INC played a major role in India's struggle for independence.
 
• The organization witnessed different phases, including the moderate phase, extremist phase, and the Gandhian phase.

questions.question: The first session of Indian National Congress took place at which of the following places?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bombay**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The first session of the Indian National Congress was held in Bombay from December 28 to December 31, 1885.
 
• The meeting was attended by 72 delegates.
 
• The session was presided over by Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee, who was the first president of the Indian National Congress.
 
• The venue for the first session was Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay.
 
• The Indian National Congress was founded by Allan Octavian Hume, a retired British civil servant.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Congress (INC)**

 
 
• The INC was formed to create a platform for civil and political dialogue among educated Indians.
 
• It played a pivotal role in the Indian independence movement against British rule.
 
• After independence, the INC became the dominant political party in India.
 
• The party initially aimed to promote moderate reforms and later shifted towards advocating for complete independence.
 
 
 
• **Allan Octavian Hume**
 
 
• He was a British administrator and one of the founders of the Indian National Congress.
 
• Hume believed that the INC would act as a 'safety valve' for the discontent among Indians, thus preventing a violent uprising.
 
• He continued to be actively involved in the INC until his death in 1912.
 
 
 
• **Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee**
 
 
• He was the first president of the Indian National Congress.
 
• Bonnerjee was a prominent lawyer and a political leader.
 
• He served as president of the INC twice, first in 1885 and again in 1892.
 
 
 
• **Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College**
 
 
• It was the venue for the first session of the Indian National Congress.
 
• The college is located in Bombay (now Mumbai).
 
• The choice of venue symbolized the blend of tradition and modernity that the INC aimed to achieve.

questions.question: The first President of the Indian National Congress was __________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Womesh Chandra Banerjee**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Womesh Chandra Banerjee was the first President of the Indian National Congress.
 
• He presided over the first session of the Congress held in Bombay (now Mumbai) in December 1885.
 
• He was a prominent lawyer and the chairman of the first session of the Indian National Congress.
 
• His presidency marked the beginning of the Indian National Congress as a political party to address issues related to colonial rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Congress (INC)**

 
 
• Founded in 1885, the INC was one of the two major political parties in India during the British rule and in the post-independence era.
 
• The INC played a crucial role in the Indian independence movement against British colonial rule.
 
• It was initially formed to obtain greater participation of Indians in government and later became the principal leader of the Indian independence movement.
 
• The first session of the INC was attended by 72 delegates from different parts of India.
 
 
 
• **Important Leaders of INC**
 
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji: Known as the "Grand Old Man of India" and the second President of the INC.
 
• Bal Gangadhar Tilak: A nationalist leader and a major figure in the early Indian independence movement.
 
• Gopal Krishna Gokhale: A senior leader of the INC and a social reformer who inspired Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• Jawaharlal Nehru: The first Prime Minister of independent India and a significant leader in the INC.
 
 
 
• **Sessions of the INC**
 
 
• The INC held annual sessions where members discussed and debated various issues related to colonial rule and India's future.
 
• These sessions were instrumental in formulating the strategies for the independence movement.
 
• Key resolutions like the Purna Swaraj (complete independence) resolution were passed in INC sessions.
 
 
 
• **Impact of INC**
 
 
• The INC was central to the struggle for Indian independence, organizing protests, and mobilizing the masses.
 
• It played a significant role in unifying the diverse regions and communities of India against colonial rule.
 
• The INC's efforts culminated in India's independence in 1947.

questions.question: The Khilafat committee was formed in Bombay, to defend temporal powers of Khalifa, in _________.
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**March 1919.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Khilafat Committee** was formed in **Bombay** in **March 1919**.
 
• The purpose of the committee was to **defend the temporal powers** of the **Khalifa**, the religious and political leader of the Ottoman Empire.
 
• This movement was a significant part of the **Indian independence struggle** and was supported by prominent leaders like **Mahatma Gandhi**.
 
• The Khilafat Movement aimed to show solidarity with the Muslim world and oppose the disintegration of the Ottoman Empire after World War I.
 
• The formation of the Khilafat Committee marked the beginning of a unique partnership between the **Indian National Congress** and the **Muslim League**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi**__

 __
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi** supported the Khilafat Movement as part of his strategy to unite Hindus and Muslims in the struggle for Indian independence.
 
• He saw the Khilafat Movement as an opportunity to strengthen the cause of Indian unity and independence.
 
 
 
• **Indian National Congress**__
 __
 
• The **Indian National Congress** played a significant role in supporting the Khilafat Movement, showcasing its commitment to religious and communal harmony.
 
• It helped in organizing protests and mobilizing support for the Khilafat cause.
 
 
 
• **Muslim League**__
 
 
• The **Muslim League** was actively involved in the Khilafat Movement, which aimed to preserve the Caliphate and protect Muslim interests globally.
 
• The movement helped in bridging gaps between different communities in India during the colonial period.

questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi started his famous 'Salt march' accompanied by _________ of his trusted volunteers.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**78**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Mahatma Gandhi initiated the Salt March on March 12, 1930, from his ashram in Sabarmati to the coastal village of Dandi.
 
• The march was a direct action campaign of tax resistance and nonviolent protest against the British salt monopoly.
 
• Gandhi was accompanied by 78 of his most trusted volunteers during the 24-day, 240-mile march to Dandi.
 
• The march is also known as the Dandi March or the Salt Satyagraha.
 
• This act of civil disobedience was a significant event in the Indian independence movement and garnered worldwide attention.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Salt Tax:**

 
 
• The British government in India imposed a tax on salt production and distribution, which was a basic necessity for the Indian populace.
 
• Gandhi chose to protest this tax because it affected all Indians, particularly the poor.
 
 
 
• **Nonviolent Resistance:**
 
 
• The Salt March is a prime example of Gandhi's philosophy of nonviolent resistance or satyagraha.
 
• This strategy aimed to achieve political and social goals through peaceful methods.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Salt March:**
 
 
• The Salt March mobilized millions of Indians and inspired numerous other acts of civil disobedience against British rule.
 
• It played a crucial role in uniting Indians across different regions and communities in the fight for independence.
 
 
 
• **International Response:**
 
 
• The march received extensive global coverage, bringing international attention to the Indian independence movement.
 
• It highlighted the injustices of British colonial rule and gained sympathy for the Indian cause worldwide.

questions.question: The Moplah Rebellion of 1921 took place in which of the following regions?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kerala**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Moplah Rebellion of 1921, also known as the Mappila Rebellion, took place in the Malabar region of Kerala.
 
• It was a significant uprising against British colonial rule and the feudal system.
 
• The rebellion was led by the Mappila Muslims of Kerala, who were primarily tenant farmers.
 
• The unrest was fueled by a combination of anti-colonial sentiments and agrarian discontent among the peasantry.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Malabar Rebellion**

 
 
• The rebellion began on August 20, 1921, and continued for several months.
 
• It involved violent confrontations between the rebels and the British authorities, leading to significant loss of life and property.
 
• The British government responded with harsh measures, including martial law and mass arrests.
 
• Several leaders of the rebellion, including Variyankunnath Kunjahammed Haji, were captured and executed.
 
 
 
• **Causes of the Rebellion**
 
 
• The immediate cause was the oppressive policies and high taxes imposed by the British and the landlords.
 
• Long-standing grievances related to land tenure and the exploitation of tenant farmers contributed to the unrest.
 
• Religious and cultural factors also played a role, as the Mappilas were predominantly Muslim in a predominantly Hindu region.
 
 
 
• **Impact and Legacy**
 
 
• The rebellion highlighted the deep-seated socio-economic issues in the Malabar region.
 
• It is remembered as a significant anti-colonial movement in Indian history.
 
• The rebellion also had a lasting impact on the communal relations in Kerala.

questions.question: Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) was founded in 1928 in which of the following cities?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Delhi**__**.**

__
 
• HRA to HSRA Transition: The Hindustan Republican Association (HRA) was earlier formed in 1924 to fight British rule through armed revolution.
 
• Meeting at Feroz Shah Kotla, Delhi: In September 1928, a crucial meeting of revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh, Chandrasekhar Azad, and others took place at Feroz Shah Kotla in Delhi.
 
• Foundation of HSRA: During this Delhi meeting, the HRA was restructured and renamed as the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA), adopting socialist ideals.
 
• Correct Location: Hence, Delhi (Feroz Shah Kotla) is the correct answer as the official founding place of HSRA.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hindustan Republican Association (HRA)**

 
 
• The precursor to HSRA, founded in 1924 by Ram Prasad Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, and others.
 
• The HRA was initially focused on armed resistance against British rule.
 
 
 
• **Kakori Train Robbery**
 
 
• An event in 1925 where members of the HRA looted government funds from a train.
 
• This act was intended to fund revolutionary activities and gain public attention.
 
 
 
• **Bhagat Singh**
 
 
• A prominent member of HSRA, known for his role in the Lahore Conspiracy Case.
 
• Executed in 1931 for his participation in the murder of British police officer John Saunders.
 
 
 
• **Chandrasekhar Azad**
 
 
• An important leader of HSRA who vowed never to be captured alive by the British.
 
• Died in 1931 in a shootout with the police at Alfred Park, Allahabad.
